messages.subject: flying birds  RE: [DIST-SAMP] Seabirds
parts:
Hi,

thanks for the infos.

For birds on the water, I am good as things stand.

But I think I do not fully understand the logic and content of the last
paragraph (copy pasted here)

"Also, be careful not to record as distance =3D 0 all birds flying if =
they, at
some point, crossed the transect line, because you will tend to have too
many 0 measurements and the modelling of the detection function might =
become
impossible. If the animals cross the line well beyond the vessel it =
might be
best to ignore them. This might be hard to do in practice, and some
arbitrary distance rule needs to be set up; what you want is a rule that
avoids a spike in the data that is not a reflection of the true =
detection
function, but a consequence of the undetected movement due to the =
flying."

I am also curious how much we are off (estimate wise) from the 10min
snapshot method, promoted by Mark Tasker 1984 for flying seabirds.

I think that this issue a key topic for applying DISTANCE Sampling to
seabirds.

Some of the seabird flocks, on water and flying, can be huge (basically
'uncountable'; so one need to force oneself counting on and near the =
line to
get estimates).

Another item might come up with birds sitting on water and then flying =
off;
again, large numbers.

Any input and feedback highly appreciated.

We really need to get it right with the seabirds, world-wide.

Very best
F.

Dear Jorge, List,

When dealing with clustered populations, and treating clusters as the
analysis units, the distance we need for analysis is the distance to the
geometric center of the group (see IDS book, page 13). If you use the
distance to the closest animal, you will tend to underestimate distances =
to
the cluster, and likely to overestimate abundance.

Regarding your first question, which is likely mostly related to flying
birds, take a look at pages 198-203 of IDS book. You might want to treat
birds flying separately. Sometimes, though because of the fast movement =
they
seem a considerable proportion of the population, the truth is that only =
a
small fraction of the population is in flight at any one moment. An =
approach
might be to separately estimate birds on the surface and birds flying, =
and
then combining the two estimates. Other approaches are suggested in the
above pages of IDS.

Also, be careful not to record as distance =3D 0 all birds flying if =
they, at
some point, crossed the transect line, because you will tend to have too
many 0 measurements and the modelling of the detection function might =
become
impossible. If the animals cross the line well beyond the vessel it =
might be
best to ignore them. This might be hard to do in practice, and some
arbitrary distance rule needs to be set up; what you want is a rule that
avoids a spike in the data that is not a reflection of the true =
detection
function, but a consequence of the undetected movement due to the =
flying.

Hope it helps,

Tiago

messages.author: d718c6bb1db28db2
messages.subject: Re: flying birds  RE: [DIST-SAMP] Seabirds
parts:
Mark Tasker's snapshot method is fine provided the observers can=20
estimate reliably where the boundaries of the counting box are, and=20
quickly count all the birds within it (so there isn't time for many=20
birds to fly in and out). As Tiago noted, there is a discussion of=20
these issues on pp198-203 of the Introduction to Distance Sampling=20
book. Where densities are too great to allow distance sampling, then=20
counts within a narrow strip together with strip-count estimation=20
methods is probably the sensible option for birds on the sea. For=20
flying birds, options are (1) Tasker's snapshot counts; (2) record=20
flying birds as within the strip for a strip count when they pass abeam=20
of the boat, provided they are still in the strip at that time (if they=20
have flown beyond the strip by then, they're not counted); (3) estimate=20
separately the proportion of time birds spend on the sea, then divide=20
the estimated number of birds on the sea by this proportion.

Steve Buckland
